text: Given two strings, s and t, return the number of distinct subsequences of s that equal t. A subsequence keeps relative order but can skip characters.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — distinct here means distinct subsequences, that is, distinct sets of index positions, not distinct resulting strings, right? If t appears using different positions, each one counts separately.
Exactly right — distinct index sets. Lengths go up to a thousand, and the answer is guaranteed to fit in a signed thirty-two-bit integer.

Let me run through the example. s is rabbbit, t is rabbit, and the answer is three. There are three b's in s and I need two, so it's choose which b to drop — three ways. Good, that matches my mental model of counting index sets.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would enumerate every subsequence of s, which is two to the m — hopeless at a thousand. This problem reminds me of two-string prefix DP: a table where cell i, j compares the first i characters of s with the first j characters of t. Because I'm counting, the cells combine by addition, not max or OR. So dp of i, j is the number of subsequences of the first i characters of s that equal the first j characters of t. The decision at each cell is what to do with the last character of s — take it to match the last character of t, or skip it.

If the two last characters match, the cell is the cell above — skip it — plus the cell diagonally up-left — take it. Otherwise, it's just the cell above, since I can only skip. And here's the part worth stressing — even when the characters match, I still add the skip branch. Matching doesn't force me to use this character; I might instead match that character of t against an earlier equal character in s. Those are different index sets, so both count. That's exactly why the three b's in the example give three and not one.
I notice you never read the left cell, dp of i, j minus one. LCS uses it. Why not here?

Good eye — that's the structural heart of the difference. In LCS the two strings are symmetric: I'm free to skip a character from either one, so on a mismatch I compare skip s, the up cell, against skip t, the left cell. Here t is a fixed target — every character of t must be matched, so I can never skip a t character. The only skip available is skip s, which is the up cell. There's no skip t, hence no left. It also means this table is asymmetric — swapping s and t changes the answer, unlike LCS.

Base cases pin it down. The first column is all ones: an empty t has exactly one way — take nothing. The first row is zero past the corner: an empty s can't form a non-empty t. The whole first column must be one, not just the corner — those cells feed the take branch for every row. So, the plan. One: build an m plus one by n plus one table and set the first column to one. Two: fill it row by row — on a match, up plus diagonal; otherwise, just up. Three: return the bottom-right cell. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's a straight table fill. The first loop sets the whole first column to one. Then for each pair of prefixes, if the last characters match, the cell is the cell above plus the cell up-left — skip plus take; otherwise it just copies the cell above. I return dp of m, n. One thing worth flagging — the table is unsigned long long, even though the answer fits in an int. That's deliberate.
You said the answer fits in a thirty-two-bit int, yet you're using unsigned long long. Isn't that overkill?

It looks like overkill, but it isn't — and I want to be precise about why. You guaranteed the final answer fits. You did not guarantee the intermediate cells do. Take s as thirty-five a's and t as thirty a's — a legal input. With all identical characters, each cell is a binomial coefficient, i choose j. The final cell, thirty-five choose thirty, is three hundred twenty-four thousand, six hundred thirty-two — it fits easily. But thirty-five choose seventeen is about four and a half billion, past INT_MAX, and eleven cells in that table overflow. Middle columns count shorter targets, and binomials peak in the middle. With int, those additions are signed overflow, which is undefined behaviour. Unsigned arithmetic is defined: it wraps modulo two to the sixty-four, and since the true answer fits, the final value is still exact. So it's load-bearing, not superstition.

Let's dry-run s equals babgbag, t equals bag; expected five. The cell that matters is the last one: the final g matches the g of bag, so it's the skip branch, one, plus the take branch, four — five. Those five are five distinct index sets, which I can read straight off the string. That matches. Corner cases: rabbbit and rabbit gives three. An empty t would give one. A t longer than s gives zero, with no special case — the table produces it.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is order m n, space order m n. Oh, one more thing — I can drop to order n space with a single rolling row, but then I have to iterate j right to left, because the recurrence needs the up-left cell, and going left to right would overwrite it before I read it. And if the ask changed from how many to just does t occur at all, I'd drop DP entirely for a linear two-pointer scan — counting is a genuine step up in difficulty from existence.

Excellent. Three things stood out. You nailed that distinct means index sets, not strings, up front. You explained the missing left cell through the asymmetry of the two strings instead of just omitting it. And when I challenged the unsigned long long, you produced a concrete legal input where int is undefined behaviour. Strong hire signal.
